'''''Carex sylvatica''''' is a species of [[Carex|sedge]] found in [[temperate deciduous forest|deciduous woodlands]] across Europe. It typically reaches {{convert|60|cm|abbr=on}} tall, and has an inflorescence made up of 3–5 pendent female [[spike (botany)|spikes]] and a single male spike. It is also used as a [[garden plant]], and has been [[introduced species|introduced]] to North America and New Zealand.

==Description==
''Carex sylvatica'' "resembles a small ''[[Carex pendula|C. pendula]]''",<ref name="King">{{cite book |author1=Michael King |author2=Piet Oudolf |year=1998 |title=Gardening with Grasses |publisher=[[Frances Lincoln]] |isbn=9780711212022 |page=124 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=-sIWitbvyDoC&pg=PA124}}</ref> growing to around {{convert|15|-|60|cm|0}} tall, or up to {{convert|150|cm|ft|0|abbr=on}} in exceptional cases.<ref name="Jermy">{{cite book |author1=A. C. Jermy |author2=D. A. Simpson |author3=M. J. Y. Foley |author4=M. S. Porter |year=2007 |title=Sedges of the British Isles |edition=3rd |series=BSBI Handbook No. 1 |isbn=978-0-901158-35-2 |publisher=[[Botanical Society of the British Isles]] |chapter=''Carex sylvatica'' Huds. |pages=334–336}}</ref> Its [[rhizome]]s are very short, giving the plant a densely [[:wikt:cespitose|cespitose]] (tufted) form.<ref name="Jermy"/><ref name="FNA"/> The leaves are {{convert|5|-|60|cm|abbr=on}} long, {{convert|3|-|7|mm|abbr=on}} wide<ref name="Jermy"/> and {{convert|1.0|-|1.3|mm|2|abbr=on}} thick,<ref name="FNA"/> with 17–31 parallel [[leaf vein|veins]]. The leaves have a slight keel, or are folded gently into an M-shape in cross-section.<ref name="Jermy"/>

The top half or third of the stem bears the [[inflorescence]], typically comprising 3–5 female [[spike (botany)|spikes]] and a single apical male spike,<ref name="Jermy"/> which may include a few female flowers at its base.<ref name="FNA"/> The female spikes are each {{convert|2.0|-|6.5|cm|1|abbr=on}} long, and are held dangling on long, rough [[peduncle (botany)|peduncles]], arising from within a long leaf-sheath.<ref name="Jermy"/> The male spike is much thinner, and is {{convert|1|-|4|cm|1|abbr=on}} long.<ref name="Jermy"/>
 
==Taxonomy==
''Carex sylvatica'' was [[species description|first described]] by the English botanist [[William Hudson (botanist)|William Hudson]] in his 1762 work ''[[Flora Anglica]]''.<ref>{{cite book |author=William Hudson |author-link=William Hudson (botanist) |year=1762 |title=Flora Anglica |language=Latin |chapter=''Carex'' |pages=346–354 |publisher=Londini, impensis auctoris |chapter-url=https://archive.org/stream/gulielmihudsoni01hudsgoog#page/n374/mode/2up}}</ref> [[Hybrid (biology)|Hybrids]] have been reported between ''C. sylvatica'' and ''[[Carex strigosa|C. strigosa]]'' (in France) and between ''C. sylvatica'' and ''[[Carex hirta|C. hirta]]'' (in Austria).<ref name="FNA"/> Its [[English language|English]] [[common name]] is "wood-sedge",<ref name="Jermy"/> or, in North America, "European woodland sedge".<ref name="FNA"/>

==Distribution and ecology==
''Carex sylvatica'' is found across Europe, and into parts of Asia, as far east as [[Iran]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://zoo-bclark01.zoo.ox.ac.uk/taxon/urn:kew.org:wcs:taxon:231389 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20130706204025/http://zoo-bclark01.zoo.ox.ac.uk/taxon/urn:kew.org:wcs:taxon:231389 |url-status=dead |archive-date=July 6, 2013 |title=''Carex sylvatica'' |work=eMonocot |accessdate=May 11, 2013 }}</ref> It has also been [[introduced species|introduced]] to North America, where it occurs in [[Ontario]], [[New York (state)|New York]] and [[North Carolina]], and to [[New Zealand]],<ref name="FNA">{{cite book |url=http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=1&taxon_id=242357574 |chapter=''Carex sylvatica'' Hudson, Fl. Angl. 353. 1762 |series=[[Flora of North America|Flora of North America North of Mexico]] |volume=23 |title=Magnoliophyta: Commelinidae (in part): Cyperaceae |author1=Joy Mastrogiuseppe |author2=Paul E. Rothrock |author3=A. C. Dibble |author4=A. A. Reznicek |year=2002 |publisher=[[Oxford University Press]] |isbn=978-0-19-515207-4}}</ref> where it was first recorded in 1969.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.nzpcn.org.nz/flora_details.aspx?ID=3619 |title=''Carex sylvatica'' |work=Flora |publisher=[[New Zealand Plant Conservation Network]] |accessdate=May 11, 2013}}</ref>

In its native range, ''C. sylvatica'' lives in [[temperate deciduous forest|deciduous woodlands]] on heavy soils; it is sometimes found in unwooded areas, but usually only as a relic of ancient woodland.<ref name="Jermy"/> In North America, it is generally found in disturbed areas within deciduous woodland.<ref name="FNA"/>

==Uses==
''Carex sylvatica'' can be used in gardens as [[ground cover]] under trees or shrubs.<ref name="King"/> [[Carl Linnaeus]] recorded that the [[Sami people]] used the plant as an insulating wadding.<ref>{{cite book |author=James Sowerby |author-link=James Sowerby |year=1802 |title=English botany |location=London |publisher=J. Davis |volume=14 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pEEPAAAAYAAJ&pg=RA4-PA995}}</ref>
